Unicorn
YOO-ni-korn
noun
From the Latin unicornis, “one-horned,” from unus (“one”) and cornu (“horn”), through Old French; the Authorized Version’s rendering of the Hebrew re’em, a great wild ox of the waste places, following the Septuagint’s monokeros.

Biblical Definition

The unicorn of the Authorized Version is not the horse of fable but the Hebrew re’em, a great wild ox of prodigious strength — a real beast, roaming the waste places, that no man could yoke to a plough. The AV translators followed the Septuagint’s monokeros and the Latin unicornis, “one-horned,” and gave the creature the English name then to hand. What Scripture says of it is not fabulous at all but plain: it is untamable, it is mighty, and its horns are terrible. Balaam, compelled to bless where he came to curse, says: “God brought them out of Egypt; he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn” (Num 23:22). That is the whole doctrine of the Exodus in a figure — Israel had no strength of her own, but the LORD who redeemed her was strong as the wild ox, and Balak’s enchantments could no more turn Him than a man could rein the re’em. Moses blesses Joseph with the same image: “his horns are like the horns of unicorns: with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth” (Deu 33:17). David prays out of the depth, “save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns” (Psa 22:21), and in another psalm rejoices, “my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn” (Psa 92:10). The horn is strength; the unicorn is strength unbroken; and every time the figure is used, the strength turns out to be God’s.

Webster 1828 Definition

A one-horned beast; in the KJV the Hebrew re’em, a great wild ox of untamable strength whose horns are the figure of power.

expand to see more

UNICORN, literally a one-horned animal; from the Latin unus, “one,” and cornu, “horn.”

In the KJV it renders the Hebrew re’em, a great wild ox of the waste places.

The AV followed the Septuagint’s monokeros and the Latin unicornis.

Scripture names the beast untamable, mighty, and terrible in its horns (Job 39:9-10).

Its strength figures the power of God, who brought Israel out of Egypt (Num 23:22).

Key Scripture

Num 23:22 — "God brought them out of Egypt; he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn."

Deu 33:17 — "His glory is like the firstling of his bullock, and his horns are like the horns of unicorns: with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth: and they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh."

Psa 22:21 — "Save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns."

Psa 92:10 — "But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn: I shall be anointed with fresh oil."

Modern Corruption

Skeptics point at the AV’s “unicorn” to mock Scripture as fable; but the Hebrew re’em is a real beast of real strength, and the mockery trades a question about English for a charge against inspiration.

expand to see more

Here is a live corruption, and it must be answered straight. The scoffer opens the Authorized Version, finds the word unicorn, and declares that the Bible teaches fairy tales — and from that he means to argue that Scripture is not to be trusted at all. The charge is a sleight of hand. The Hebrew word is re’em, and what the text says of the creature is the opposite of fable: it is a beast of enormous strength that cannot be bound with his band in the furrow nor trusted to bring home the seed (Job 39:9-10), whose horns push the nations to the ends of the earth. That is a description of a living animal in the waste places, and the mocker never engages it. The AV translators, following the Septuagint’s monokeros and the Latin unicornis, rendered a great one-horned wild ox with the English word then available for a one-horned beast. Whether a later English word would serve the modern reader better is a question about English; it is not a question about inspiration. The scoffer swaps the one for the other and hopes no one notices.

So the line must be drawn on both sides, and drawn honestly. We concede nothing on inerrancy: the Word of God given in the Hebrew and the Greek is without error, and no man has yet shown an error in the re’em. Neither do we pretend that the KJV’s English is beyond all revision — it is a translation, made by men, out of a providentially preserved text, and its renderings are as revisable as the English tongue itself. To confound the two is the very confusion the mocker trades upon: a question of vocabulary is dressed up as a verdict against the Holy Ghost. What Scripture affirms is the strength, and the strength stands. The LORD brought Israel out of Egypt with the strength of an unicorn, and neither the enchantments of Balaam nor the wit of the scoffer can turn Him. It is better to fear that strength than to laugh at the word chosen for it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a one-horned beast; in Scripture, the wild ox of untamable strength.

expand to see more

Unicorn — Latin unicornis, from unus and cornu, “one horn.”

It renders the Hebrew re’em, a great wild ox of the waste places.

The AV followed the Septuagint’s monokeros in the rendering.

Scripture names the beast untamable and mighty, terrible in its horns.

Its strength is the figure of God’s power in the Exodus (Num 23:22).

Usage

"God brought them out of Egypt; He hath as it were the strength of an unicorn — redemption by a might not our own."

"My horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn: the saint’s strength is a gift, not a possession."

"The re’em cannot be bound in the furrow; the mocker’s fable is not the Bible’s beast."
